At the edge of town, where the road forgot its purpose, there was a little shop that sold umbrellas.

It sold them only on sunny days.

The owner, a woman named Mara, claimed this was because people bought umbrellas more thoughtfully when they weren’t afraid of getting wet. They came in, shook the handles, tested the hinges, and chose colors they could imagine carrying through a storm. On rainy days, she said, everyone bought the first one they saw.

Mara had one umbrella she never sold. It was yellow, with a wooden handle polished smooth by years of use. Whenever the clouds gathered, she stood in the doorway holding it closed, watching the street darken.

One afternoon, a boy came in while the sun was still bright. He had no money, but he looked at every umbrella carefully.

“What are you looking for?” Mara asked.

“Something for my father,” he said. “He’s been gone a long time. But he promised he’d come back when it rained.”

Mara looked up at the cloudless sky. Then she took the yellow umbrella from the stand and placed it in his hands.

“Keep it open,” she said.

The boy stepped outside and raised it above his head.

For a moment, nothing happened. Then the first raindrop fell—softly, like someone remembering.
